\section{An incomplete metric in a big class}
\label{sec:incomplete-divisorial-metric}

The ample locus of a big closed class is the complement of its non-K\"ahler locus. A positive solution of a Monge--Amp\`ere equation on this locus need not define a complete metric. We give an explicit example in which the minimal divisorial singularity cancels the pole of an exponential equation. The question of completeness for this equation is raised in \cite[Question~3.5]{DNGL26}. The example concerns arbitrary big classes and divisors; the additional compatibility conditions arising from a K\"ahler--Ricci flow require separate analysis.

In this section $\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta)$ denotes the classical finite-energy class for a big closed class on a compact K\"ahler manifold, relative to a potential with minimal singularities; see \cite[Section~2]{BEGZ10}. We retain the book's convention $\ddc=\mathrm{i}\partial\bar\partial/(2\pi)$, so that $\ddc\log|t|^2=[t=0]$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:incomplete-divisorial-metric}
There exist a smooth projective surface $Y$, a smooth irreducible divisor $E$, a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta$ with big class $\alpha$, a Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_Y(E)$, a defining section $\sigma$, and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_Y$ with the following properties. The equation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:incomplete-divisorial-equation}
 \left\langle(\theta+\ddc\rho)^2\right\rangle
 =\mathrm{e}^{\rho}|\sigma|^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}V_Y
\end{equation}
has a unique solution $\rho\in\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta)$, and this solution has minimal singularities. Moreover,
\[
 \operatorname{Amp}(\alpha)=Y\setminus E
\]
is precisely the open locus on which $\theta+\ddc\rho$ is smooth and strictly positive. Its restriction to every nonempty connected open subset of $Y\setminus E$ is incomplete. In particular, no dense Zariski open subset carries a complete induced metric.
\end{theorem}

We first prove the elementary extension estimate used to identify the minimal singularities. Let $p=[1:0:0]\in\mathbb P^2$, and let $\omega_2$ be the Fubini--Study form given in affine coordinates by
\[
 \omega_2=\ddc\log(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2).
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:projective-puncture-upper-bound}
Every $\omega_2$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2\setminus\{p\}$ is bounded above there.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For such a function $v$, the function
$h=v+\log(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)$ is plurisubharmonic on a punctured bidisc $\Delta_R^2\setminus\{0\}$. Choose $0<r<R$. The compact set
\[
 K=\{|z_1|\leq r,\ |z_2|=r\}
\]
avoids the puncture, so $h\leq M$ on $K$ for a finite $M$. For each $0<|z_1|\leq r$, the subharmonic maximum principle in the $z_2$-disc gives $h(z_1,z_2)\leq M$ for $|z_2|\leq r$. For $z_1=0$ and $0<|z_2|<r$, apply the maximum principle in the $z_1$-disc, whose boundary is already covered by this bound. Thus $v$ is bounded above near $p$. Upper semicontinuity and compactness bound it on the complement of a smaller neighborhood.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{thm:incomplete-divisorial-metric}]
\emph{The surface and the divisor.}
Use the incidence model
\[
 Y=\{([Z_0:Z_1:Z_2],[W_1:W_2])\in\mathbb P^2\times\mathbb P^1:
           Z_1W_2=Z_2W_1\}.
\]
The projections $\pi:Y\to\mathbb P^2$ and $q:Y\to\mathbb P^1$ identify $Y$ with the blow-up at $p$, with exceptional divisor $E=\pi^{-1}(p)$. Write
\[
 \beta=\pi^*\omega_2,\qquad \gamma=q^*\omega_1,
 \qquad \Omega=\beta+\gamma,
\]
where $\omega_1$ has the same Fubini--Study normalization. The form $\Omega$ is K\"ahler, being the restriction of the product metric.

The projection $(Z_0,Z_1,Z_2)\mapsto(Z_1,Z_2)$ gives a section $\sigma$ of
\[
 \pi^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)\otimes q^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1).
\]
Indeed, its image belongs to the tautological line represented by $[W_1:W_2]$. The section vanishes simply along $E$, identifying this line bundle with $\mathcal O_Y(E)$. For the product of the Fubini--Study and induced tautological metrics, its squared norm is
\[
 s=|\sigma|^2=
 \frac{|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}.
\]
In a blow-up chart $\pi(t,w)=(t,tw)$ and $q(t,w)=[1:w]$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:incomplete-divisor-norm}
 s=\frac{|t|^2(1+|w|^2)}{1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)},
 \qquad \ddc\log s=[E]+\gamma-\beta.
\end{equation}
The current identity follows either from this formula and the second blow-up chart or from Poincar\'e--Lelong.

\emph{The big class and its equation.}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:incomplete-current}
 \theta=3\beta-2\gamma,\qquad \rho=2\log s,
 \qquad T=\theta+\ddc\rho=\beta+2[E].
\end{equation}
Thus $\rho\in\PSH(Y,\theta)$. The class $\alpha=\{\theta\}$ is big: the potential $\psi=(5/2)\log s$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:incomplete-strict-current}
 \theta+\ddc\psi
 =\tfrac12(\beta+\gamma)+\tfrac52[E]\geq\tfrac12\Omega.
\end{equation}
It is not nef, since $\int_E\theta=-2$: the restriction of $\beta$ to $E$ vanishes and $q|_E$ is an isomorphism to $\mathbb P^1$. A nef class has nonnegative degree on every curve by its defining smooth approximations.

On $Y\setminus E$ define $\mathrm{d}V_Y=\beta^2/s$. To check extension across $E$, put
\[
 \mathrm{d}\lambda_{t,w}
 =\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}2\mathrm{d}t\wedge\mathrm{d}\bar t
       \wedge\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}2\mathrm{d}w\wedge\mathrm{d}\bar w.
\]
The normalized Fubini--Study volume on $\mathbb P^2$ is
\[
 \omega_2^2=\frac{2}{\pi^2}
 \frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda_{z_1,z_2}}{(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)^3}.
\]
Since the complex Jacobian of $(t,w)\mapsto(t,tw)$ is $t$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \beta^2&=\frac{2}{\pi^2}
 \frac{|t|^2\,\mathrm{d}\lambda_{t,w}}
      {[1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)]^3},\\
 \mathrm{d}V_Y&=\frac{2}{\pi^2}
 \frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda_{t,w}}
      {(1+|w|^2)[1+|t|^2(1+|w|^2)]^2}.
\end{align*}
The second expression is smooth and strictly positive at $t=0$. Interchanging the two homogeneous coordinates gives the extension on the other chart. The extensions agree off $E$, hence everywhere on their overlap.

The non-pluripolar product of $T$ agrees with $\beta^2$ off $E$ and gives no mass to $E$. The smooth measure $\beta^2$ also gives no mass to $E$, so
\[
 \langle T^2\rangle=\beta^2,
 \qquad
 \mathrm{e}^{\rho}|\sigma|^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}V_Y
   =s^2s^{-1}\frac{\beta^2}{s}=\beta^2.
\]
The right side of \eqref{eq:incomplete-divisorial-equation} is defined on $Y\setminus E$ and extended by zero on $E$; no product of zero and infinity is taken there. This proves the equation and gives $\int_Y\langle T^2\rangle=\int_{\mathbb P^2}\omega_2^2=1$.

\emph{Minimal singularities and energy.}
For $u\in\PSH(Y,\theta)$, the function $u-\rho$ on $Y\setminus E$ descends to an $\omega_2$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^2\setminus\{p\}$, because
\[
 \beta+\ddc(u-\rho)=\theta+\ddc u\geq0
 \quad\text{on }Y\setminus E.
\]
By \cref{lem:projective-puncture-upper-bound}, $u\leq\rho+C_u$ there. Near $E$, \eqref{eq:incomplete-divisor-norm} gives $u(t,w)\leq2\log|t|^2+O(1)$. Add a smooth local potential of the closed form $\theta$, restrict to a transverse disc, and apply the submean inequality at its center. Letting the radius tend to zero shows that $u=-\infty$ on $E$. The comparison therefore holds on all of $Y$, proving minimality.

Let $V_\theta$ be the normalized minimal envelope. Since $s\leq1$, minimality gives
\[
 \rho\leq V_\theta\leq\rho+C.
\]
Thus $\rho-V_\theta$ is bounded off $E$. The defining relative energy is
\[
 E_\theta(\rho)=\frac13\sum_{j=0}^2
 \int_Y(\rho-V_\theta)
 \left\langle(\theta+\ddc\rho)^j\wedge
                (\theta+\ddc V_\theta)^{2-j}\right\rangle.
\]
The mixed measures have finite mass in the closed K\"ahler theory and do not charge $E$. Hence $E_\theta(\rho)>-\infty$, so $\rho\in\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta)$. Here we use the standard finiteness of non-pluripolar products and the finite-energy definition in \cite[Proposition~1.6 and Section~2.2]{BEGZ10}. A potential with minimal singularities has full mass; in this example that mass is $1$.

\emph{Uniqueness.}
Suppose $u\in\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta)$ is another solution, and let $\mathrm{d}\mu=s^{-1}\mathrm{d}V_Y$ on $Y\setminus E$, extended by zero on $E$. This measure is locally smooth and positive off $E$, but has infinite total mass. The full-mass comparison principle \cite[Corollary~2.3]{BEGZ10} gives
\[
 \int_{\{u<\rho\}}\mathrm{e}^{\rho}\,\mathrm{d}\mu
 \leq\int_{\{u<\rho\}}\mathrm{e}^{u}\,\mathrm{d}\mu.
\]
Both integrals are finite, since the two Monge--Amp\`ere measures have mass $1$. The strictly larger integrand on the left forces $\mu(\{u<\rho\})=0$. Interchanging $u$ and $\rho$ gives $\mu(\{\rho<u\})=0$ as well. They therefore agree almost everywhere for smooth volume on $Y\setminus E$, and hence on $Y$, since $E$ has zero smooth volume. Equality of the canonical upper-semicontinuous representatives of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions gives $u=\rho$ everywhere.

\emph{The ample locus and incompleteness.}
The current in \eqref{eq:incomplete-strict-current} is smooth off $E$, while every global $\theta$-plurisubharmonic potential is $-\infty$ on $E$. Thus no K\"ahler current in $\alpha$ can be smooth near a point of $E$. The characterization in \cref{thm:bc-non-kahler-locus} gives
\[
 \operatorname{Amp}(\alpha)=Y\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha)
 =Y\setminus E.
\]
The current $T$ equals $\beta$ there and is strictly positive because $\pi$ is a biholomorphism away from $E$. Its nonzero divisorial part $2[E]$ prevents smoothness at every point of $E$.

Let $U\subset Y\setminus E$ be nonempty and connected, and set $W=\pi(U)$. The map $\pi:(U,T|_U)\to(W,\omega_2|_W)$ is an isometry. Choose $x\in W$ and a smooth path $c:[0,1]\to\mathbb P^2$ from $x$ to $p$. Its first exit time
\[
 t_0=\min\{t\in[0,1]:c(t)\notin W\}
\]
is positive, and $c([0,t_0))\subset W$. This path has finite Fubini--Study length. For $t_k\nearrow t_0$, its tail lengths show that $c(t_k)$ is Cauchy for the intrinsic metric of $W$. It has no limit there: intrinsic convergence implies ambient convergence, whose limit is $c(t_0)\notin W$. Thus $U$ is incomplete. Applying this argument to each connected component proves the assertion for a possibly disconnected dense Zariski open set.
\end{proof}

The cancellation $\mathrm{e}^{\rho}|\sigma|^{-2}=s$ leaves the deleted point at finite distance. Consequently, the big-class exponential equation with an arbitrary smooth divisor does not force completeness, even for its unique finite-energy solution with minimal singularities. The example has a non-nef class and does not settle the same question with a nef hypothesis. It also does not settle a flow conjecture in which the class, divisor and singularity coefficients must arise from specified initial data; compare \cite[Section~3.1]{DNGL26}.

\section{Connections with non-K\"ahler geometry}
\label{sec:non-kahler-geometric-problems}

The general theory should explain geometric obstructions as well as solve equations. We describe six connections. In each case the distinction between a closed Bott--Chern class and an arbitrary smooth background is essential. The literature statements below are recorded with their hypotheses; the subsequent questions ask what the constructions of this book could add.

\subsection{Nef classes, bigness and the Fujiki class}

A compact complex manifold belongs to the Fujiki class $\mathcal C$ if it is bimeromorphic to a compact K\"ahler manifold. The classical characterization by the existence of a closed K\"ahler current is due to Demailly--P\u aun \cite[Theorem 0.6 in the arXiv version]{DP04}. Their transcendental Grauert--Riemenschneider conjecture asks whether a closed nef real $(1,1)$-class $\alpha$ with
\[
 \int_X\alpha^n>0
\]
is big on an arbitrary compact complex manifold. Equivalently in this situation, the proposed conclusion is $X\in\mathcal C$; compare \cite[Conjecture 0.7 in the arXiv version]{DP04}.

The bounded mass property is closely tied to this problem. Under exactly the preceding nefness and positive top-intersection hypotheses, Guedj--Lu prove
\[
 \alpha\text{ is big}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_+(h)<\infty
\]
for a Hermitian metric $h$ \cite[Theorem 4.9]{GL22}. Boucksom--Guedj--Lu also characterize $\mathcal C$ by bounded mass together with positivity of their upper class volume for some closed Bott--Chern class \cite[Theorem C]{BGL25}. That upper volume is not the invariant $\mathcal V_\mu$ defined here.

The failure of bounded mass on the Hopf threefold does not refute the Demailly--P\u aun conjecture. A counterexample would also need a closed nef class with positive top self-intersection. Conversely, a proof of the conjecture cannot impose bounded mass as an unexplained general fact. The Hermitian framework must account for why that property follows in the particular geometry forced by such a class.

The elliptic threefold of \cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} supplies the complementary test: it has bounded mass, but no big closed class. Its entire nef cone is the nonnegative span of two smooth rank-one classes, and every top self-intersection is zero, by \cref{prop:elliptic-bott-chern-cones}. Hence this lower-mass example also leaves the geometric conjecture untouched. The exact boundary calculation in \cref{prop:elliptic-boundary-volume} describes its degeneration without identifying a nonclosed metric with a closed class.

The volume of this book separates two possible steps:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dp-two-bridges}
 \int_X\alpha^n>0
 \quad\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}\quad
 \mathcal V_\mu(\alpha)>0
 \quad\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}\quad
 \alpha\text{ is big}.
\end{equation}
Neither arrow is established here in the unrestricted compact complex setting. The second is the closed special case of \cref{conj:nef-gaud-volume-big}. On a compact K\"ahler manifold both follow from the usual nef volume formula and the classical nef-and-big criterion. Without closedness, positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu$ cannot characterize $\mathcal C$: every Hermitian metric $h$ already satisfies $\mathcal V_\mu(h)>0$, on every compact complex manifold.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:closed-nef-gaud-bridge}
Let $\alpha$ be closed and nef with $\int_X\alpha^n>0$. Prove a positive lower bound for $\lambda_\mu(\alpha)$, and rule out the collapse in \cref{prop:gaud-positive-volume-collapse} for a sequence minimizing the bigness threshold of $\alpha$.
\end{problem}

This is a proposed route to the geometric conjecture, not a claimed weaker substitute already known to suffice automatically. The relevant test metrics can be normalized by $\int_Xh\wedge\gamma^{n-1}=1$. A positive lower bound for $D_\mu(\gamma)$ along one threshold-minimizing sequence would finish the second step. The Gauduchon equation can change the volume density while retaining an Aeppli class. Since $\alpha$ is closed, it also retains the numerator paired against $\alpha$. The missing estimate is control of the trace normalization and determinant denominator after that change. Merely prescribing a volume density does not give this estimate.

\subsection{Positive lower volume and concentration}

Positive lower mass fails in general. The threefold in \cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} has $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian metric, while \cref{prop:lower-mass-balanced-metric} supplies a balanced metric with finite upper mass. The Hopf threefold gives the opposite combination, $v_-(h)=6$ and $v_+(h)=\infty$ in its stated normalization. The upper and lower mass properties are independent.

For $n\geq2$, the determinant measures give an exact analytic formulation. Fix a smooth positive probability measure $\mathrm{d}V$, and write
\[
 \Gamma_0(T)=k_T\,\mathrm{d}V,\qquad T\in\mathscr G_h.
\]
By \cref{thm:gaud-determinant-endpoint},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric}
 v_-(h)>0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \sup_{T\in\mathscr G_h}
       \|k_T\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}<\infty.
\end{equation}
The exact supremum is $v_-(h)^{-1/n}$, including the value $+\infty$. Uniform estimates for every smaller exponent $1<q<n/(n-1)$ hold without either volume property. The lower-mass example violates the endpoint already for smooth strictly positive tests. Thus positivity, $\ddc T=0$ and normalized trace alone do not control concentration at that exponent.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:geometric-gaud-endpoint}
Find geometric conditions that imply the endpoint estimate in \eqref{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric}, and identify how they exclude the concentration mechanism of \cref{sec:vanishing-lower-mass}. For a fixed smooth density, determine whether the smaller family of maximizing Gauduchon currents admits stronger estimates than the full normalized cone.
\end{problem}

The balanced condition and bounded upper mass are insufficient, even together. The explicit identity \eqref{eq:lower-mass-vertical-energy} relates the failing lower bound to a vertical Dirichlet integral on an elliptic fibration. Meanwhile the positive exact form $\alpha\wedge\beta$ excludes pluriclosed metrics and closed K\"ahler currents. These calculations supply geometric information about this example without giving a classification of all lower-mass degeneration.

The equation consequence is exact for a Hermitian background: \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-solvability} characterizes positive lower mass by solvability for all finite non-pluripolar measures. When it vanishes, even a positive $L^1$ density bounded away from zero can admit no positive scaled subsolution. The remaining equation questions concern specified measures or additional geometric hypotheses, and separately the effect of the exponential weight.

\subsection{Null loci and the singularities of the Chern--Ricci flow}

For a big smooth background $\theta$, Dang defines its non-Hermitian locus $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta)$ as the intersection of the singular sets of all strict currents in that background with \emph{almost analytic singularities}; this intersection is itself attained by such a current \cite[Definition 2.12 and Theorem 2.14]{DangNull26}. In the source's terminology the potential is locally a positive multiple of the logarithm of an ideal norm, up to a bounded remainder, and on a suitable log resolution its remainder after subtracting the divisorial logarithms is smooth \cite[Definition 2.8]{DangNull26}. We retain this exact singularity condition.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
For nef and big $\theta$, define
\[
 \operatorname{Null}(\theta)
 =\bigcup_{\substack{V\subset X\text{ irreducible analytic}\\
                     \dim V>0,\ \theta|_V\text{ not big}}}V.
\]
Bigness on a singular subvariety uses its intrinsic analytic definition. Dang proves $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta)=\operatorname{Null}(\theta)$ for arbitrary compact complex $X$ and nef, big, possibly nonclosed $\theta$ \cite[Theorem 1.1]{DangNull26}. This qualitative identification is therefore a known theorem. Detecting bigness and this locus from numerical data is a further issue: the same paper's Theorem A uses bounded mass on $X$ and positive lower volume on its positive-dimensional submanifolds.

Theorem C of \cite{DangNull26} identifies finite-time Chern--Ricci singularities with the null locus under positive limiting lower volume, for arbitrary initial metrics in dimension two, and for Guan--Li initial metrics in higher dimensions. Here Guan--Li means $\ddc\omega_0=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega_0\wedge \dc\omega_0=0$. These hypotheses must not be silently replaced by positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu$.

The current calculation in \cref{cor:chern-ricci-current-lifetime} applies without those extra hypotheses. At a finite maximal time $\tau$, the background $\theta_\tau=\omega_0-\tau\operatorname{Ric}(\omega_0)$ is nef. Its normalized annihilating currents satisfy
\[
 \int_X\theta_\tau\wedge T=0.
\]
If $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta_\tau)>0$, their determinant-weighted measures vanish by \cref{prop:nef-annihilator-determinant}. This is a precise degeneracy statement, but it does not imply that their traces are concentrated on analytic sets. A smooth positive semidefinite matrix of deficient rank can be defined on an open set.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\begin{problem}\label{qu:chern-ricci-gaud-singularities}
Suppose a Chern--Ricci flow has finite maximal time $\tau$ and $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta_\tau)>0$. Can one prove that $\theta_\tau$ is big and that the flow converges smoothly to a positive metric locally on $X\setminus E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta_\tau)$, without a bounded mass hypothesis? How do the annihilating Gauduchon currents describe the resulting degeneracy?
\end{problem}

The first assertion is a case of the volume-to-bigness question. Once bigness of $\theta_\tau$ is known, \cite[Theorem 4.3]{DangNull26} already supplies convergence as currents and smooth local convergence off $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta_\tau)$, by parabolic estimates. Combined with nefness and the qualitative null-locus theorem, this identifies the analytic exceptional set. Thus the missing step in this route is the proposed numerical criterion for bigness. The local envelope continuity and homogeneous replacement arguments of \cref{thm:big-continuous-envelope-contact} supply an elliptic foundation away from a strict barrier's poles; they are not a reconstruction of the cited parabolic estimates.

\subsection{Degenerate densities and uniqueness}

The counterexample in \cref{thm:degenerate-hermitian-nonuniqueness} shows that a smooth nonnegative density can have two distinct smooth normalized solutions even on $\mathbb P^3$. The further construction in \cref{thm:numa-thin-zero-set} has uncountably many smooth normalized solutions and a density positive off two real hypersurfaces. By modifying the background, \cref{thm:quadratic-density-nonuniqueness} achieves exactly quadratic vanishing on those hypersurfaces. Thus neither zero smooth volume of the zero set nor finite-order vanishing suffices for uniqueness. All the backgrounds are strictly Hermitian and have bounded mass; their non-Hermitian loci are empty. The degeneration causing nonuniqueness belongs to the density and the solution forms, and is not detected by the background's null locus.

This places a necessary restriction on any geometric use of the equation. A construction that assigns a canonical potential to arbitrary nonnegative data must specify a selection procedure and prove that it is well defined. Existence in the ordinary minimal singularity type does not provide such a selection. The unique scalar, and the corresponding variational volume for strictly positive data, remain meaningful without uniqueness of every potential. On a compact Hermitian surface, \cref{uni-cor:dense-lowdim} proves uniqueness for $C^2$ potentials and continuous density positive on a dense set, with no differential condition on the metric. In dimension three, \cref{uni-thm:sobolev} instead uses a sign condition on $\ddc\omega$. The cofactor identity in \eqref{eq:mixed-uniqueness-defect} and the signed quadratic-difference argument provide two distinct integration mechanisms.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:density-zero-set-uniqueness}
Let $X$ be connected, $\omega$ Hermitian and $f\geq0$ smooth. Suppose $\{f>0\}$ is connected and dense. Are two bounded normalized solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u)=cf\,\mathrm{d}V$, with the same $c>0$, necessarily equal? Separately, for densities allowing nonuniqueness, do the solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u_\lambda)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda}f\,\mathrm{d}V$ converge uniformly after subtracting their suprema, as $\lambda\downarrow0$?
\end{problem}

For $C^{1,1}$ potentials the first question is answered affirmatively by \cref{uni-thm:anchors}. The remaining issue is the passage to bounded potentials. All the hypersurface counterexamples here have three positive-density components; even the analytic density in \cref{uni-thm:analytic-example} has exactly this topology. The second asks for a canonical limit, and does not follow from uniqueness of the positive-exponent equation at each fixed parameter. A selection could exist even when the limiting equation has several solutions. These counterexamples do not refute \cref{conj:continuous-gaud-adjoint}: that conjecture uses a finite continuous logarithmic density $F$, for which $\mathrm{e}^F$ is strictly positive. The logarithms of the degenerate densities have no finite continuous extensions across their zero sets.

There is already some control of selection in the Hermitian $L^p$ setting: \cref{prop:symmetric-equation-clusters} proves uniform precompactness of the normalized approximations, and every cluster limit preserves the symmetries of the data. For the symmetric projective example, the radial argument of \cref{thm:numa-selected-limit} goes further: the whole normalized family converges uniformly to the explicit symmetric $C^{1,1}$ solution of \cref{prop:numa-radial-continuum}. Thus this example has both many normalized solutions and a definite limit for the specified approximation. The general selection question above remains open in this treatment.

For a nonzero density at positive threshold in dimension at least two, \cref{cor:smooth-dual-exact-equation,cor:smooth-dual-exponential-limit} give uniqueness of the normalized threshold solution and uniform convergence of the whole normalized positive-exponent family whenever a smooth strictly positive maximizing Gauduchon current exists. The construction in \cref{ex:nonclosed-dual-zero-density} satisfies this condition even though the density vanishes on an open set. Thus the size of the zero set alone does not determine uniqueness; the dual condition also involves the background.

\subsection{Balanced and pluriclosed metrics}

A Hermitian metric $\beta$ is balanced if $\mathrm{d}\beta^{n-1}=0$, while a Hermitian metric $\omega$ is pluriclosed if $\ddc\omega=0$. The Fino--Vezzoni conjecture asks whether a compact complex manifold admitting both types of metrics is K\"ahler; the two metrics can be different. See \cite[Conjecture 1.1]{FV26} for the statement and recent context. A single metric satisfying both conditions is already K\"ahler, which does not resolve the question with two metrics.

Chiose proves that a compact manifold in $\mathcal C$ admitting a pluriclosed metric is K\"ahler \cite[Theorem 0.2 in the author manuscript]{Chiose14}. Consequently, in the balanced--pluriclosed setting, it would suffice to construct a closed big $(1,1)$-current and apply the characterization of $\mathcal C$. This route emphasizes a geometric existence problem which is absent when one only works with an arbitrary Hermitian background.

There is an elementary obstruction to using the scalar equation alone. For every distributional potential $u$,
\[
 \mathrm{d}(\omega+\ddc u)=\mathrm{d}\omega.
\]
Thus if the starting pluriclosed metric is nonclosed, no potential in its fixed background makes it K\"ahler. The finite-volume equation, including its smooth solution, does not change this differential datum. Similarly, a conformal Gauduchon representative need not be balanced. Positivity and a scalar normalization cannot be used to replace either missing closedness condition.

The balanced form $\beta^{n-1}$ nevertheless supplies more than a Gauduchon test: it pairs trivially with every exact real two-form by Stokes. It therefore interacts with flows whose variation has an exact component. Fino--Vezzoni propose long-time existence and convergence to a K\"ahler metric for the pluriclosed flow when a balanced metric exists and $c_1(X)=0$ \cite[Conjecture 1.2]{FV26}. Their invariant examples illustrate the use of a conserved balanced trace. In general that integral is not a pointwise metric bound.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:balanced-pluriclosed-program}
Use the coexistence of a balanced metric and a pluriclosed metric to construct closed positive data, or to control a geometric flow that can change the torsion. Determine what estimate beyond the finite balanced trace prevents metric degeneration. Can determinant estimates for Gauduchon currents contribute to that estimate?
\end{problem}

This asks for an interaction with the scalar theory, not an implication already proved by its equation. One can first study families for which the balanced trace and the determinant density are explicitly controlled. The passage from an integral trace bound to local ellipticity is then a concrete analytic target. No such passage for arbitrary families is asserted here.

\subsection{Morse inequalities and the choice of volume}

The closed K\"ahler theory provides a demanding comparison. Tosatti's recent preprint establishes the transcendental Morse inequality
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(\alpha-\beta)
 \geq\int_X\alpha^n-n\int_X\alpha^{n-1}\wedge\beta
\]

\section{Connections with non-K\"ahler geometry}
\label{sec:non-kahler-geometric-problems}

The general theory should explain geometric obstructions as well as solve equations. We describe six connections. In each case the distinction between a closed Bott--Chern class and an arbitrary smooth background is essential. The literature statements below are recorded with their hypotheses; the subsequent questions ask what the constructions of this book could add.

\subsection{Nef classes, bigness and the Fujiki class}

A compact complex manifold belongs to the Fujiki class $\mathcal C$ if it is bimeromorphic to a compact K\"ahler manifold. The classical characterization by the existence of a closed K\"ahler current is due to Demailly--P\u aun \cite[Theorem 0.6 in the arXiv version]{DP04}. Their transcendental Grauert--Riemenschneider conjecture asks whether a closed nef real $(1,1)$-class $\alpha$ with
\[
 \int_X\alpha^n>0
\]
is big on an arbitrary compact complex manifold. Equivalently in this situation, the proposed conclusion is $X\in\mathcal C$; compare \cite[Conjecture 0.7 in the arXiv version]{DP04}.

The bounded mass property is closely tied to this problem. Under exactly the preceding nefness and positive top-intersection hypotheses, Guedj--Lu prove
\[
 \alpha\text{ is big}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_+(h)<\infty
\]
for a Hermitian metric $h$ \cite[Theorem 4.9]{GL22}. Boucksom--Guedj--Lu also characterize $\mathcal C$ by bounded mass together with positivity of their upper class volume for some closed Bott--Chern class \cite[Theorem C]{BGL25}. That upper volume is not the invariant $\mathcal V_\mu$ defined here.

The failure of bounded mass on the Hopf threefold does not refute the Demailly--P\u aun conjecture. A counterexample would also need a closed nef class with positive top self-intersection. Conversely, a proof of the conjecture cannot impose bounded mass as an unexplained general fact. The Hermitian framework must account for why that property follows in the particular geometry forced by such a class.

The elliptic threefold of \cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} supplies the complementary test: it has bounded mass, but no big closed class. Its entire nef cone is the nonnegative span of two smooth rank-one classes, and every top self-intersection is zero, by \cref{prop:elliptic-bott-chern-cones}. Hence this lower-mass example also leaves the geometric conjecture untouched. The exact boundary calculation in \cref{prop:elliptic-boundary-volume} describes its degeneration without identifying a nonclosed metric with a closed class.

The volume of this book separates two possible steps:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dp-two-bridges}
 \int_X\alpha^n>0
 \quad\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}\quad
 \mathcal V_\mu(\alpha)>0
 \quad\stackrel{?}{\Longrightarrow}\quad
 \alpha\text{ is big}.
\end{equation}
Neither arrow is established here in the unrestricted compact complex setting. The second is the closed special case of \cref{conj:nef-gaud-volume-big}. On a compact K\"ahler manifold both follow from the usual nef volume formula and the classical nef-and-big criterion. Without closedness, positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu$ cannot characterize $\mathcal C$: every Hermitian metric $h$ already satisfies $\mathcal V_\mu(h)>0$, on every compact complex manifold.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:closed-nef-gaud-bridge}
Let $\alpha$ be closed and nef with $\int_X\alpha^n>0$. Prove a positive lower bound for $\lambda_\mu(\alpha)$, and rule out the collapse in \cref{prop:gaud-positive-volume-collapse} for a sequence minimizing the bigness threshold of $\alpha$.
\end{problem}

This is a proposed route to the geometric conjecture, not a claimed weaker substitute already known to suffice automatically. The relevant test metrics can be normalized by $\int_Xh\wedge\gamma^{n-1}=1$. A positive lower bound for $D_\mu(\gamma)$ along one threshold-minimizing sequence would finish the second step. The Gauduchon equation can change the volume density while retaining an Aeppli class. Since $\alpha$ is closed, it also retains the numerator paired against $\alpha$. The missing estimate is control of the trace normalization and determinant denominator after that change. Merely prescribing a volume density does not give this estimate.

\subsection{Positive lower volume and concentration}

Positive lower mass fails in general. The threefold in \cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} has $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian metric, while \cref{prop:lower-mass-balanced-metric} supplies a balanced metric with finite upper mass. The Hopf threefold gives the opposite combination, $v_-(h)=6$ and $v_+(h)=\infty$ in its stated normalization. The upper and lower mass properties are independent.

For $n\geq2$, the determinant measures give an exact analytic formulation. Fix a smooth positive probability measure $\mathrm{d}V$, and write
\[
 \Gamma_0(T)=k_T\,\mathrm{d}V,\qquad T\in\mathscr G_h.
\]
By \cref{thm:gaud-determinant-endpoint},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric}
 v_-(h)>0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \sup_{T\in\mathscr G_h}
       \|k_T\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}<\infty.
\end{equation}
The exact supremum is $v_-(h)^{-1/n}$, including the value $+\infty$. Uniform estimates for every smaller exponent $1<q<n/(n-1)$ hold without either volume property. The lower-mass example violates the endpoint already for smooth strictly positive tests. Thus positivity, $\ddc T=0$ and normalized trace alone do not control concentration at that exponent.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:geometric-gaud-endpoint}
Find geometric conditions that imply the endpoint estimate in \eqref{eq:pvp-endpoint-geometric}, and identify how they exclude the concentration mechanism of \cref{sec:vanishing-lower-mass}. For a fixed smooth density, determine whether the smaller family of maximizing Gauduchon currents admits stronger estimates than the full normalized cone.
\end{problem}

The balanced condition and bounded upper mass are insufficient, even together. The explicit identity \eqref{eq:lower-mass-vertical-energy} relates the failing lower bound to a vertical Dirichlet integral on an elliptic fibration. Meanwhile the positive exact form $\alpha\wedge\beta$ excludes pluriclosed metrics and closed K\"ahler currents. These calculations supply geometric information about this example without giving a classification of all lower-mass degeneration.

The equation consequence is exact for a Hermitian background: \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-solvability} characterizes positive lower mass by solvability for all finite non-pluripolar measures. When it vanishes, even a positive $L^1$ density bounded away from zero can admit no positive scaled subsolution. The remaining equation questions concern specified measures or additional geometric hypotheses, and separately the effect of the exponential weight.

\subsection{Null loci and the singularities of the Chern--Ricci flow}

For a big smooth background $\theta$, Dang defines its non-Hermitian locus $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta)$ as the intersection of the singular sets of all strict currents in that background with \emph{almost analytic singularities}; this intersection is itself attained by such a current \cite[Definition 2.12 and Theorem 2.14]{DangNull26}. In the source's terminology the potential is locally a positive multiple of the logarithm of an ideal norm, up to a bounded remainder, and on a suitable log resolution its remainder after subtracting the divisorial logarithms is smooth \cite[Definition 2.8]{DangNull26}. We retain this exact singularity condition.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
For nef and big $\theta$, define
\[
 \operatorname{Null}(\theta)
 =\bigcup_{\substack{V\subset X\text{ irreducible analytic}\\
                     \dim V>0,\ \theta|_V\text{ not big}}}V.
\]
Bigness on a singular subvariety uses its intrinsic analytic definition. Dang proves $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta)=\operatorname{Null}(\theta)$ for arbitrary compact complex $X$ and nef, big, possibly nonclosed $\theta$ \cite[Theorem 1.1]{DangNull26}. This qualitative identification is therefore a known theorem. Detecting bigness and this locus from numerical data is a further issue: the same paper's Theorem A uses bounded mass on $X$ and positive lower volume on its positive-dimensional submanifolds.

Theorem C of \cite{DangNull26} identifies finite-time Chern--Ricci singularities with the null locus under positive limiting lower volume, for arbitrary initial metrics in dimension two, and for Guan--Li initial metrics in higher dimensions. Here Guan--Li means $\ddc\omega_0=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega_0\wedge \dc\omega_0=0$. These hypotheses must not be silently replaced by positivity of $\mathcal V_\mu$.

The current calculation in \cref{cor:chern-ricci-current-lifetime} applies without those extra hypotheses. At a finite maximal time $\tau$, the background $\theta_\tau=\omega_0-\tau\operatorname{Ric}(\omega_0)$ is nef. Its normalized annihilating currents satisfy
\[
 \int_X\theta_\tau\wedge T=0.
\]
If $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta_\tau)>0$, their determinant-weighted measures vanish by \cref{prop:nef-annihilator-determinant}. This is a precise degeneracy statement, but it does not imply that their traces are concentrated on analytic sets. A smooth positive semidefinite matrix of deficient rank can be defined on an open set.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\begin{problem}\label{qu:chern-ricci-gaud-singularities}
Suppose a Chern--Ricci flow has finite maximal time $\tau$ and $\mathcal V_\mu(\theta_\tau)>0$. Can one prove that $\theta_\tau$ is big and that the flow converges smoothly to a positive metric locally on $X\setminus E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta_\tau)$, without a bounded mass hypothesis? How do the annihilating Gauduchon currents describe the resulting degeneracy?
\end{problem}

The first assertion is a case of the volume-to-bigness question. Once bigness of $\theta_\tau$ is known, \cite[Theorem 4.3]{DangNull26} already supplies convergence as currents and smooth local convergence off $E_{\mathrm{nH}}(\theta_\tau)$, by parabolic estimates. Combined with nefness and the qualitative null-locus theorem, this identifies the analytic exceptional set. Thus the missing step in this route is the proposed numerical criterion for bigness. The local envelope continuity and homogeneous replacement arguments of \cref{thm:big-continuous-envelope-contact} supply an elliptic foundation away from a strict barrier's poles; they are not a reconstruction of the cited parabolic estimates.

Completeness requires an additional metric estimate. In \cref{thm:incomplete-divisorial-metric}, the unique finite-energy solution of a divisorial exponential equation in a big closed class is incomplete on every nonempty connected open subset of its ample locus. Its minimal divisorial singularity cancels the prescribed pole. This resolves the unrestricted big-class completeness question negatively; it does not decide completeness under nefness or under the compatibility conditions of the geometric smoothing problem in \cite[Section~3.1]{DNGL26}. In particular it does not settle \cref{qu:chern-ricci-gaud-singularities}, whose limiting background is nef.

\subsection{Degenerate densities and uniqueness}

The counterexample in \cref{thm:degenerate-hermitian-nonuniqueness} shows that a smooth nonnegative density can have two distinct smooth normalized solutions even on $\mathbb P^3$. The further construction in \cref{thm:numa-thin-zero-set} has uncountably many smooth normalized solutions and a density positive off two real hypersurfaces. By modifying the background, \cref{thm:quadratic-density-nonuniqueness} achieves exactly quadratic vanishing on those hypersurfaces. Thus neither zero smooth volume of the zero set nor finite-order vanishing suffices for uniqueness. All the backgrounds are strictly Hermitian and have bounded mass; their non-Hermitian loci are empty. The degeneration causing nonuniqueness belongs to the density and the solution forms, and is not detected by the background's null locus.

This places a necessary restriction on any geometric use of the equation. A construction that assigns a canonical potential to arbitrary nonnegative data must specify a selection procedure and prove that it is well defined. Existence in the ordinary minimal singularity type does not provide such a selection. The unique scalar, and the corresponding variational volume for strictly positive data, remain meaningful without uniqueness of every potential. On a compact Hermitian surface, \cref{uni-cor:dense-lowdim} proves uniqueness for $C^2$ potentials and continuous density positive on a dense set, with no differential condition on the metric. In dimension three, \cref{uni-thm:sobolev} instead uses a sign condition on $\ddc\omega$. The cofactor identity in \eqref{eq:mixed-uniqueness-defect} and the signed quadratic-difference argument provide two distinct integration mechanisms.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:density-zero-set-uniqueness}
Let $X$ be connected, $\omega$ Hermitian and $f\geq0$ smooth. Suppose $\{f>0\}$ is connected and dense. Are two bounded normalized solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u)=cf\,\mathrm{d}V$, with the same $c>0$, necessarily equal? Separately, for densities allowing nonuniqueness, do the solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u_\lambda)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda}f\,\mathrm{d}V$ converge uniformly after subtracting their suprema, as $\lambda\downarrow0$?
\end{problem}

For $C^{1,1}$ potentials the first question is answered affirmatively by \cref{uni-thm:anchors}. The remaining issue is the passage to bounded potentials. All the hypersurface counterexamples here have three positive-density components; even the analytic density in \cref{uni-thm:analytic-example} has exactly this topology. The second asks for a canonical limit, and does not follow from uniqueness of the positive-exponent equation at each fixed parameter. A selection could exist even when the limiting equation has several solutions. These counterexamples do not refute \cref{conj:continuous-gaud-adjoint}: that conjecture uses a finite continuous logarithmic density $F$, for which $\mathrm{e}^F$ is strictly positive. The logarithms of the degenerate densities have no finite continuous extensions across their zero sets.

There is already some control of selection in the Hermitian $L^p$ setting: \cref{prop:symmetric-equation-clusters} proves uniform precompactness of the normalized approximations, and every cluster limit preserves the symmetries of the data. For the symmetric projective example, the radial argument of \cref{thm:numa-selected-limit} goes further: the whole normalized family converges uniformly to the explicit symmetric $C^{1,1}$ solution of \cref{prop:numa-radial-continuum}. Thus this example has both many normalized solutions and a definite limit for the specified approximation. The general selection question above remains open in this treatment.

For a nonzero density at positive threshold in dimension at least two, \cref{cor:smooth-dual-exact-equation,cor:smooth-dual-exponential-limit} give uniqueness of the normalized threshold solution and uniform convergence of the whole normalized positive-exponent family whenever a smooth strictly positive maximizing Gauduchon current exists. The construction in \cref{ex:nonclosed-dual-zero-density} satisfies this condition even though the density vanishes on an open set. Thus the size of the zero set alone does not determine uniqueness; the dual condition also involves the background.

A Hermitian metric $\beta$ is balanced if $\mathrm{d}\beta^{n-1}=0$, while a Hermitian metric $\omega$ is pluriclosed if $\ddc\omega=0$. The Fino--Vezzoni conjecture asks whether a compact complex manifold admitting both types of metrics is K\"ahler; the two metrics can be different. See \cite[Conjecture 1.1]{FV26} for the statement and recent context. A single metric satisfying both conditions is already K\"ahler, which does not resolve the question with two metrics.

Chiose proves that a compact manifold in $\mathcal C$ admitting a pluriclosed metric is K\"ahler \cite[Theorem 0.2 in the author manuscript]{Chiose14}. \[
 \mathrm{d}(\omega+\ddc u)=\mathrm{d}\omega.
\]

The finite-volume equation, including its smooth solution, does not change this differential datum. Similarly, a conformal Gauduchon representative need not be balanced. It therefore interacts with flows whose variation has an exact component. Fino--Vezzoni propose long-time existence and convergence to a K\"ahler metric for the pluriclosed flow when a balanced metric exists and $c_1(X)=0$ \cite[Conjecture 1.2]{FV26}. Their invariant examples illustrate the use of a conserved balanced trace. In general that integral is not a pointwise metric bound.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:balanced-pluriclosed-program}
Use the coexistence of a balanced metric and a pluriclosed metric to construct closed positive data, or to control a geometric flow that can change the torsion. Determine what estimate beyond the finite balanced trace prevents metric degeneration. Can determinant estimates for Gauduchon currents contribute to that estimate?
\end{problem}

This asks for an interaction with the scalar theory, not an implication already proved by its equation. One can first study families for which the balanced trace and the determinant density are explicitly controlled. The passage from an integral trace bound to local ellipticity is then a concrete analytic target. No such passage for arbitrary families is asserted here.
